claimBoundary: This is one provenance-bound Codex pass. It is single-model evidence, not human, instructor, independent, classroom, or multi-judge validation.

claims: A list is an ordered collection of values written in square brackets; each element has an index, beginning at 0.
A list is written with square brackets [] holding comma-separated values.
Individual elements are accessed directly using an index.
Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence.
A for loop can iterate through a list, visiting each element in order.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §3.4 List basics; §9.1 Modifying and iterating lists

artifact.q: A lab program needs to visit each item in a list of labeled data one by one. What method best fits that task?
op: Use a for loop to step through the list
Access the last item with index 1
artifact.ex: Use a for loop to step through the list is correct because a for loop can iterate through a list and visit each element in order. The index-1 option is the most plausible misconception because list indexes begin at 0, not 1.

artifact.q: If a list has a length of 5, what is the highest valid index for an element?
op: 4 (since indexes end one less than length)
artifact.ex: Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence.

claims: A string is a sequence of characters indexed from left to right starting at 0; slicing extracts a contiguous substring with the [a:b] notation.
For a string s, the left-most character is index 0 and the right-most is index len(s) - 1.
Negative indexing refers to characters from right to left starting at -1.
A slice s[a:b] returns characters from index a (inclusive) up to index b (exclusive).
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §1.4 String basics; §8.2 String slicing

artifact.q: If a string $s$ has a length of 5, what is the index of the right-most character?
artifact.ex: Option 4 is incorrect because the right-most character is at index len(s) - 1, which is 4 for a string of length 5. Option 2 is correct because the right-most character is at index len(s) - 1, which is 4 for a string of length 5.

artifact.q: In Python, if s = "studio", which expression returns the substring "tud"?
artifact.ex: s[1:4] is correct because slicing includes the start index 1 and stops before index 4, giving characters at positions 1, 2, and 3. The most plausible mistake is choosing s[0:3], which also has three characters but starts one position too early and returns "stu" instead.

claims: A for loop iterates over each element of a container — a range of numbers, a string, or a list — binding a loop variable to one element at a time.
A container can be a range of numbers, a string of characters, or a list of values.
The loop retrieves the objects of a container one at a time.
range() produces a sequence of integers and is commonly paired with a for loop to repeat the body a fixed number of times; range(n) yields 0 through n-1.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §5.2 For loop

artifact.q: Which action describes the fundamental operation of a for loop?
op: Binding a loop variable to one element at a time.
Retrieving objects of a container one at a time.
Iterating over each element of a container.
artifact.ex: Binding a loop variable to one element at a time.

artifact.q: In a program that processes the characters in the word "code", what does the for loop do?
op: It steps through each character in order, one at a time.
It stores the whole word inside the loop variable at once.
It changes the word into a range of integers automatically.
It repeats forever until the word becomes a list.
artifact.ex: A for loop iterates over the string one element at a time, binding the loop variable to each character in turn. The most plausible misconception is that the loop variable holds the entire string at once, but the loop retrieves container objects individually instead.

claims: Igneous rock forms when molten magma or lava cools and crystallizes; how fast it cools controls crystal size, distinguishing coarse intrusive rocks from fine-grained extrusive rocks.
Lava cooling quickly at the surface forms tiny crystals, while magma cooling slowly at depth forms large crystals.
Magma that cools slowly deep within the crust forms intrusive (plutonic) rock with a coarse-grained texture.
Lava cooling at or near the surface forms extrusive (volcanic) rock with a fine-grained texture.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §4.1 Magma generation and igneous textures

artifact.df: Rock formed when molten material cools slowly beneath the Earth's surface.
artifact.mi: Rock formed by rapid cooling at the surface.
artifact.cx: Rock formed by slow cooling deep within the crust.

artifact.df: An igneous rock that crystallizes below Earth’s surface during slow cooling.
artifact.eg: Granite forming from magma that solidifies deep in the crust.
artifact.mi: It is the same as lava that cools on the surface.
artifact.cx: Intrusive rocks are plutonic and typically have coarse-grained textures because crystals have time to grow.

claims: Earth is layered into a thin outer crust, a thick rocky mantle, and a metallic core; the upper mantle's asthenosphere is solid rock that flows slowly by convection.
The mantle sits below the crust and above the core.
The core has both liquid and solid layers and is made mostly of iron and nickel.
The asthenosphere is mechanically weak and flows by convection currents driven by the core's heat.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §2.1 Earth's interior

artifact.q: A student describes a region of the upper mantle as solid rock that flows slowly because of convection. Which layer is being described?
artifact.ex: The asthenosphere is correct because it is mechanically weak solid rock that moves slowly by convection currents driven by heat from the core. A plausible misconception is the lithosphere, but that layer is not the one identified here as the flowing upper mantle region.

artifact.q: What material primarily composes the core layers?
artifact.ex: Iron and nickel is the correct answer because the core is made mostly of these materials (Claim 2). The most plausible misconception is selecting silicates, which are characteristic of the crust and mantle, not the core.

claims: In music theory, a scale is "any consecutive series of notes that form a progression between one note and its octave", typically by order of pitch or fundamental frequency.
A measure of the width of each scale step provides a method to classify scales.
Scales can be abstracted from performance or composition.
Therefore, any scale is distinguishable by its "step-pattern", or how its intervals interact with each other.
A specific scale is defined by its characteristic interval pattern and by a special note, known as its first degree (or tonic).
The expression scale degree refers to these numerical labels.

artifact.q: A student sorts note collections while studying scales. Which choice best matches the theory definition?
op: A consecutive series of notes that progresses between one note and its octave.
Any unordered set of pitches used in a melody.
A chord built from three stacked notes.
A repeated rhythm pattern across a measure.
artifact.ex: Correct: a scale is a consecutive series of notes spanning an octave. Misconception: any collection of pitches qualifies; order and octave span are part of the definition.

artifact.q: How can scales be analyzed in relation to their structure?
op: By the numerical labels assigned to the notes.
By the measure of the width of each scale step.
By abstracting them from performance or composition.
By the way their intervals interact with each other.
artifact.ex: By the way their intervals interact with each other.

claims: In music, a triad is a set of three notes (or "pitch classes") that can be stacked vertically in thirds.
A seventh chord is a chord consisting of a triad plus a note forming an interval of a seventh above the chord's root.
The seventh destabilized the triad, and allowed the composer to emphasize movement in a given direction.
There are four different inversions of a seventh chord.

artifact.q: In a short progression, one sonority is used to soften stability and push the music forward. Which chord type is most associated with that effect?
artifact.ex: The seventh chord is linked to added instability and directional motion, whereas a triad is the more stable three-note stack. A plausible misconception is to treat any stacked three-note sonority as equally forward-driving.

artifact.q: How does the addition of a seventh note affect a triad?
op: A) It maintains the triad's stability without changing its vertical stacking.
b) It destabilizes the triad and emphasizes movement in a given direction.
c) It creates a new triad consisting of only three notes.
d) It results in four different inversions of the original chord.
artifact.ex: Option B is correct because the seventh destabilizes the triad and allows the composer to emphasize movement. Option A is incorrect because the seventh destabilizes the triad, and Option C is incorrect because the seventh chord is not a triad.

claims: In Western musical notation, the staff (UK usually stave); (plural: staves), also occasionally referred to as a pentagram, is a set of horizontal lines (usually five) with spaces between them, that each represent a different musical pitch.
Which staff positions represent which notes is determined by a clef placed at the beginning of the staff.
A clef (from French: clef 'key') is a musical symbol used to indicate which notes are represented by the lines and spaces on a musical staff.
The treble clef is also the upper staff of the grand staff used for harp and keyboard instruments.
Bass clef is the bottom clef in the grand staff for harp and keyboard instruments.

artifact.q: What is the primary function of a clef in Western musical notation?
op: To define the horizontal lines on the staff.
To indicate which notes are represented by the lines and spaces.
To determine the pitch represented by each space.
To show the relationship between different musical pitches.
artifact.ex: The correct choice indicates that a clef is a symbol used to indicate which notes are represented by the lines and spaces on a musical staff. The misconception is that a clef defines the lines themselves, which is incorrect; the lines and spaces are the staff structure.

artifact.q: In a grand staff for keyboard notation, which clef names the upper staff?
artifact.ex: Treble clef is the upper staff of the grand staff; bass clef is the bottom clef. The common misconception is to swap them because both appear in grand-staff notation.

claims: Journey mapping represents an end-to-end experience from the user's perspective so a team can see connected steps, boundaries, breakdowns, and opportunities.
A journey map should start from research about the steps users actually take and the transactions involved.
An experience map should make struggle points and candidate improvement areas visible.
A map can reveal dead ends where the user cannot continue toward the larger goal.
Journey analysis should include gaps between online and offline parts of a service.

artifact.df: A research-backed way to chart the user's full experience from start to finish, including boundaries, breakdowns, and opportunities.
artifact.eg: In the capstone, students could map how someone signs up, submits a request, switches between web and phone support, and reaches the final outcome.
artifact.mi: It is just a flowchart of interface screens.
artifact.cx: The correction is that it focuses on the user's end-to-end experience, not only screens or system steps.

artifact.df: A visual representation of the complete user path.
artifact.eg: Mapping the entire process from initial search to final purchase.
artifact.mi: Thinking a map only shows the main features.
artifact.cx: It shows connected steps, boundaries, breakdowns, and opportunities.

claims: A UX research plan turns a decision need into actionable learning objectives, participants, tasks, evidence-capture roles, and a rehearsal-ready study setup.
The team should agree what it wants to learn from the research round before selecting study details.
A prototype used in research should work end-to-end and be usable and accessible in the research venue.
Researchers should run through test tasks on the day before the research session.
A practice session with a team member can expose procedure problems before participants arrive.

artifact.df: A study arrangement that has been checked so the tasks, participants, evidence capture, and venue can be used smoothly.
artifact.eg: Before the session, the team confirms the prototype works end-to-end and runs the tasks with a teammate.
artifact.mi: Once the prototype exists, the session can proceed without any practice.
artifact.cx: Check the flow ahead of time; a practice run can expose procedure problems before participants arrive.

artifact.df: The preparation of the study environment and tasks prior to participant arrival.
artifact.eg: Running through test tasks on the day of the research session.
artifact.mi: Assuming rehearsal is only necessary for the participants.
artifact.cx: Researchers should run through test tasks on the day before the research session.
